rationale:
TRIAGE: All three deserve head-to-head comparison because they represent two distinct endpoint definitions and two sibling models within the same study family.

- PGS001033 is the only candidate directly aligned to the target trait EFO (“blood coagulation disease”) and reports clean, comparable discrimination metrics including PRS-only AUROC/R² plus full-model AUROC with conventional covariates. Its time-to-event phenotyping and larger validation N also make it a strong direct-endpoint anchor, even though the label is broader (“Other coagulation defects”).

- PGS002034 and PGS001826 share the same reported phenotype (“Congenital deficiency of other clotting factors…”) and publication/cohort context, but differ materially in method and variant count (LDpred2 with many variants vs penalized regression with few variants). Their reported performance is partial correlation (partial-r) rather than AUROC/R², which can mislead a single-shot picker if compared naively against AUROC-based records; nonetheless, they are cleaner PRS-style summaries within their study family and are near-ties to each other (very similar partial-r with overlapping CIs). Keeping both enables a fair sibling comparison and prevents overcommitting to one based on method label or variant count alone.

Downstream comparison should explicitly separate (a) endpoint alignment (blood coagulation disease vs congenital deficiency subtype) from (b) predictive evidence comparability (AUROC/R² vs partial-r) and (c) within-family sibling choice (PGS001826 vs PGS002034). Uncertainty: Cross-candidate metric comparability is limited because PGS001033 reports AUROC/R² (including PRS-only), while PGS001826/PGS002034 report partial-r only; without a shared metric axis, apparent performance differences may reflect reporting format rather than true predictive strength. Endpoint mismatch between the congenital-deficiency phenotype and the broader blood-coagulation-disease target could also dominate transfer suitability, but the records alone do not resolve how close these endpoints are in practice. LEGACY_PROPOSAL: All three candidates are direct matches at the broad level of coagulation disorders, but none is a clean, high-confidence match for the generic target label "blood coagulation disease." PGS001033 maps directly to the target EFO (blood coagulation disease) and provides PRS-comparable metrics including PGS-only AUROC (0.634) and PGS R² (0.0578), with only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/array), which is stronger visible performance evidence than the other two models. However, its endpoint is "Other coagulation defects (time-to-event)" and it comes from a pan-trait UK Biobank sparse-score framework ("across 813 traits"), which domain guidance flags as a generalizability risk; additionally it is extremely sparse (1 variant), raising concern about capturing polygenic signal. The alternatives (PGS001826, PGS002034) are for a narrower congenital clotting-factor deficiency EFO (not the broad coagulation disease umbrella) and report only partial correlation (~0.056) without AUROC/R², making them hard to compare and not clearly better despite being less sparse (especially PGS002034). Given these tradeoffs and limited endpoint fidelity for the broad target, the best available direct-match is PGS001033 but with low confidence. PICK: Keeping the legacy proposal is still defensible on the visible evidence. Among all candidates, PGS001033 is the only record whose trait_efo exactly matches the target (“blood coagulation disease”) and it also provides the most directly comparable predictive evidence (PGS-only AUROC 0.634 and PGS-only R² 0.0578, plus full-model AUROC 0.656 with conventional covariates age/sex/PCs/array). It also has a substantially larger validation sample size (n=67,425) than the congenital-deficiency scores (n=19,864), which strengthens the stability of the reported discrimination.

PGS001826 and PGS002034 are direct matches only at a narrower subtype level (their trait_efo is congenital vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors deficiency; trait_reported is congenital deficiency of other clotting factors). They report only partial correlation (~0.056 with overlapping CIs) and no AUROC/R², so they do not present stronger visible discrimination/effect evidence than PGS001033; between them they are near-tied, with PGS002034 a slight runner-up due to essentially identical partial-r but much broader variant coverage.

Overall, none is a clean high-quality match for the generic target label (endpoint heterogeneity across candidates, and PGS001033’s “other coagulation defects (time-to-event)” plus extreme sparsity of 1 variant). Still, given exact EFO alignment and the strongest/cleanest visible performance reporting, PGS001033 remains the best-supported direct-match pick, but only at low confidence. CRITIC: No visible contradiction found with keeping PGS001033. It is the only candidate whose trait_efo exactly matches the target trait (“blood coagulation disease”), and it provides directly comparable predictive evidence including PGS-only AUROC (0.634, with CI) and PGS-only R² (0.0578), plus a full-model AUROC (0.656, CI) with conventional covariates (age, sex, PCs, array). It also has a larger validation sample size (n=67,425) than the two congenital-deficiency candidates (n=19,864), supporting more stable reported discrimination.

The alternatives (PGS001826, PGS002034) target a narrower EFO (congenital vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors deficiency) and report only partial correlation (~0.056 with overlapping CIs) without AUROC/R², so there is no stronger visible predictive evidence that would justify revising away from the exact-EFO, AUROC-reported candidate. Between those two, they are near-tied; PGS002034 has far more variants but essentially identical partial-r, which is insufficient to displace PGS001033 given endpoint/EFO alignment and richer performance reporting.

Known weaknesses of PGS001033 remain (endpoint label “Other coagulation defects (time-to-event)” and extreme sparsity: 1 variant; pan-trait UKB framework), but these are not concrete visible disqualifiers and do not create a better-supported alternative among the provided records. The legacy_with_domain_proposal already selected PGS001033; it is not more defensible than the proposed_pick because they agree.

TRIAGE: All three candidates are direct-endpoint Crohn’s disease scores and should be compared head-to-head.

- PGS004254 deserves close comparison because it reports much stronger apparent discrimination (full-model AUROC 0.72 with tight CI; also reports an OR 2.18). However, its reported AUROC is not explicitly PRS-only (no PRS-only AUC/R² fields populated), so it could mislead a single-shot picker if the performance is materially driven by covariates or a different evaluation setup. Still, the endpoint label is direct and the covariates listed (age/sex/PCs) look conventional, so it should remain a top shortlist item rather than being penalized for metric packaging.

- PGS001331 and PGS001330 are sibling models from the same UKB snpnet paper with clean PRS-only metrics reported (PGS-only AUROC/R² plus full-model and incremental AUROC). They are plausible near-ties and should be compared because small differences in AUROC/incremental AUROC and phenotype definition could matter downstream.
  - PGS001331 has slightly higher PRS-only AUROC and higher full-model/incremental AUROC than PGS001330 in the selected European validation, making it the stronger of the two on the visible metrics.
  - PGS001330 uses a time-to-event phenotype label (“time-to-event”), which could be meaningfully different from the binary case/control framing in PGS001331; that endpoint framing difference is exactly the kind of detail that can mislead a single-shot picker if ignored, so it should stay in close comparison despite slightly weaker metrics.

Overall: shortlist all three to explicitly resolve (a) PRS-only vs full-model comparability (PGS004254 vs the snpnet siblings) and (b) phenotype framing differences (TTE vs non-TTE) within the snpnet siblings. Uncertainty: Key uncertainty is metric comparability for PGS004254: AUROC is reported only as “full-model” with no PRS-only breakdown, so its apparent advantage may not be directly comparable to the PRS-only AUROCs in PGS001330/PGS001331. Another uncertainty is endpoint definition differences (time-to-event vs binary) between PGS001330 and PGS001331, which may affect which metric is most relevant for downstream use even if both are labeled Crohn’s disease. LEGACY_PROPOSAL: All three candidates are direct matches to Crohn disease (trait_efo and phenotyping_reported align). PGS001330 is a time-to-event endpoint (explicit warning signal vs generic disease risk) and comes from a pan-trait UK Biobank framework paper (“across 813 traits”), with only modest PRS-only metrics (PGS AUROC ~0.576; PGS R2 ~0.006). PGS001331 is also from the same pan-trait framework family but uses a straightforward Crohn’s disease endpoint and shows slightly better PRS-only metrics than PGS001330 (PGS AUROC ~0.579; PGS R2 ~0.0068; incremental AUROC ~0.027). PGS004254 is endpoint-faithful (Crohn’s disease), uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (LDpred2-auto) with far more variants, and reports a strong effect size (OR 2.18 per SD) plus a high AUROC (0.72) with only basic covariates; however, the AUROC appears to be a full-model metric (no explicit PGS-only AUROC/R2 provided), making cross-model comparability uncertain. Given the structural advantages and strong OR evidence, PGS004254 is the best-supported direct-match candidate, but missing PRS-only metrics and differing study context keep the overall direct-match recommendation sub-optimal rather than high-confidence. PICK: All candidates are direct matches to Crohn’s disease (trait_efo aligns; phenotyping_reported is Crohn’s disease for PGS001331/PGS004254 and Crohn’s disease [regional enteritis] TTE for PGS001330).

Keeping the legacy proposal (PGS004254) remains defensible because it shows substantially stronger visible predictive signal in its evaluation: AUROC 0.72 (tight CI 0.70–0.73) and an OR 2.18 (2.05–2.32), with conventional covariates (age, sex, PCs). Although its AUROC is reported as a full-model metric (no explicit PRS-only AUC/R² fields populated), the covariate set is ordinary and similar in spirit to the snpnet siblings’ packaging, so the strong discrimination/effect evidence is still compelling rather than being dismissed on metric-format grounds.

Among the snpnet siblings, PGS001331 is the stronger runner-up: it uses a straightforward Crohn’s disease endpoint (not time-to-event) and has slightly better PRS-only and full-model metrics than PGS001330 (PGS-only AUROC 0.579 vs 0.576; incremental AUROC 0.027 vs 0.024). PGS001330 is third because its time-to-event framing is a mild endpoint mismatch versus a generic disease-risk use, and its metrics are slightly weaker.

Overall label remains DIRECT_SUB_OPTIMAL because the top pick’s reported performance is not cleanly separated into PRS-only vs covariate-added components, making cross-candidate comparability less certain even though the endpoint match and visible signal are strong. CRITIC: No visible contradiction found with keeping PGS004254 as the top direct-match pick.

Visible record check:
- Endpoint/trait alignment: All three candidates are direct matches on trait_efo (Crohn disease). PGS004254 and PGS001331 have straightforward Crohn’s disease phenotyping_reported; PGS001330 is explicitly time-to-event (TTE) Crohn’s disease [regional enteritis], which is a mild endpoint framing mismatch versus generic case/control risk.
- Predictive evidence: PGS004254 shows substantially stronger visible evaluation signal (AUROC 0.72, CI 0.70–0.73; OR 2.18, CI 2.05–2.32) than the snpnet siblings’ reported AUCs (~0.60 full-model; ~0.58 PGS-only). Although PGS004254’s AUROC is only populated under full_model_auc (PRS-only fields are null), the listed covariates (age, sex, PCs) are conventional and similar in spirit to the siblings’ covariate sets, so there is no clear visible packaging/leakage red flag that would invalidate using the reported AUROC/OR as supportive evidence.
- Sample sizes/ancestry: PGS004254 has smaller training n (12,331) than the snpnet UKB models (269,704), but similar validation scale (22,296 vs 24,905) and clean EUR evaluation. This does not create a concrete reason to overturn the much stronger visible discrimination/effect evidence.

Legacy vs proposed: The legacy_with_domain_proposal and proposed_pick both select PGS004254; there is no better-supported visible alternative that clearly beats it. Among the remaining two, PGS001331 remains the better runner-up than PGS001330 based on slightly stronger metrics and non-TTE endpoint framing.

Therefore, keep PGS004254 with DIRECT_SUB_OPTIMAL due to metric comparability uncertainty (full-model-only reporting) but strong visible performance.

TRIAGE: Two main publication families with multiple siblings warrant head-to-head comparison rather than single-shot picking.

1) 2024-12-16 Nat Genet family (PGS004946–PGS004951): These provide PRS-only AUC (and AUPRC) plus delta PRS/residual R²-style increments, which are comparatively clean for isolating PRS contribution even though multiple R² definitions are reported. Within this family, MTAG siblings generally show stronger PRS-only discrimination/effect sizes than their non-MTAG counterparts, creating plausible near-ties that could flip depending on whether the downstream PICK prioritizes endpoint fidelity (non-MTAG) vs integrated power (MTAG).
- Strongest-looking within-family candidates to compare closely: PGS004949 (MTAG; PRS-only AUC 0.68; OR 1.91; large validation n=326,106) and PGS004951 (MTAG; PRS-only AUC 0.67; OR 1.93; smaller validation n=7,761). These are near-tied on PRS-only AUC/OR but differ materially in validation scale and possibly phenotype packaging.
- Also keep PGS004947 and PGS004946 as near-ties: both are evaluated in MAE (100%) with PRS-only AUC 0.66 vs 0.65 and similar ORs; they differ by MTAG vs non-MTAG and have the same validation n=96,016. This pair is a classic “could mislead” situation if one only looks at a single metric.
- PGS004950 and PGS004948 are retained on watchlist: they are non-MTAG siblings with weaker PRS-only AUC (0.64) but have different phenotype labels (“Clinical dilated cardiomyopathy” for PGS004950 vs “Non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy” for PGS004948) and different validation sizes (7,761 vs 326,106). They are plausible alternatives if downstream prioritizes a specific endpoint label or cohort context.

2) 2024-04-18 Nat Genet family (PGS004861–PGS004862): These are clean, direct “Dilated cardiomyopathy” labels with large European validation (n=347,585) and conventional covariates. However, performance is reported as full-model AUROC/R² (no explicit PRS-only AUROC), which can mislead comparisons against the later family that reports PRS-only metrics. Keep both for downstream comparison as “clean-label, large-N, full-model-metric” baselines.
- PGS004862 (MTAG) slightly edges PGS004861 on full-model AUROC (0.71 vs 0.70) and OR (1.76 vs 1.56), making them a near-tie pair worth direct comparison.

Overall, shortlist preserves: (a) strongest PRS-only performers (PGS004949/PGS004951), (b) MTAG vs non-MTAG near-ties within the same evaluation setting (PGS004947/PGS004946), and (c) large-N direct-label alternatives with full-model metrics (PGS004862/PGS004861). Watchlist keeps the remaining siblings that could become preferred depending on endpoint-label preference (clinical vs non-ischemic) or if downstream decides to emphasize validation scale vs metric type. Uncertainty: Cross-family comparability is limited because PGS004861/PGS004862 report full-model AUROC/R² (with age/sex/PC covariates) while the 2024-12-16 family reports multiple R² definitions plus explicit PRS-only AUC/AUPRC and delta metrics; downstream should avoid over-interpreting small AUROC differences across these reporting regimes. Endpoint labels differ across the 2024-12-16 siblings (“clinical” vs “non-ischemic”), and evaluation ancestry differs (EUR-only vs MAE-only), so the apparent best candidate may depend on which endpoint/transport context downstream prioritizes. LEGACY_PROPOSAL: All 8 candidates are direct matches to the target trait (dilated cardiomyopathy) by trait_reported/trait_efo, with phenotyping_reported spanning generic DCM, non-ischemic DCM, and clinical DCM. Following the provided domain guidance, endpoint fidelity is primary and MTAG variants are mildly preferred within the same study family. Among the MTAG models, PGS004951 targets clinical dilated cardiomyopathy (high endpoint fidelity for a generic DCM target) and shows the strongest visible effect-size evidence (OR=1.93 per SD) with a competitive univariate (PRS-only) AUC=0.67; its covariates are basic (sex, PC1-12), reducing concern about covariate-inflated performance. Main limitation: the candidate pool mixes different endpoint definitions (clinical vs non-ischemic vs unspecified DCM) and evaluation contexts/ancestries, and several non-ischemic MTAG siblings (e.g., PGS004949) have similar PRS-only AUC with much larger validation size, making the choice not unequivocal from metadata alone. PICK: All candidates are direct matches by trait_reported/trait_efo. The legacy proposal (PGS004951) is defensible on endpoint label (“Clinical dilated cardiomyopathy”) and strong effect/discrimination (PRS-only AUC 0.67; OR 1.93), but the full candidate list contains a visibly better-supported near-twin: PGS004949. PGS004949 (MTAG) shows slightly stronger PRS-only discrimination (AUC 0.68, CI 0.66–0.69) with similarly strong effect size (OR 1.91) and is validated at much larger scale (n=326,106) with conventional covariates (age, age^2, sex, array, PC1-12). Although its phenotyping_reported is “Non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy” (a subtype label vs the generic target), it remains within the same direct DCM construct and the combination of stronger PRS-only AUC plus far larger validation support makes it the best-supported direct-match overall. PGS004951 remains a close runner-up due to the ‘clinical’ endpoint label and comparable PRS-only performance but is supported by a much smaller validation sample (n=7,761). The older Nat Genet family scores (PGS004861/PGS004862) have very large validation (n=347,585) and clean covariates, but their reported AUROC/R² are full-model (not clearly PRS-only), making them less directly comparable to the PRS-only evidence available for PGS004949/PGS004951. CRITIC: Proposed_pick PGS004949 is defensible vs visible alternatives. It is a direct match on trait_reported/trait_efo and has explicit PRS-only discrimination reported (univariate AUC 0.68, CI 0.66–0.69) plus strong effect size (OR 1.91). It is also supported by a much larger validation sample (n=326,106) than the legacy pick PGS004951 (n=7,761), and its covariates (age, age^2, sex, array, PC1-12) are conventional with no obvious packaging/leakage signals in the metadata.

Legacy_with_domain_proposal PGS004951 remains defensible (clinical DCM label; PRS-only AUC 0.67; OR 1.93; relatively clean covariates), but there is no visible contradiction that would force reverting to it: PGS004949’s phenotype label is “Non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy,” which is still within the direct DCM construct, and it has slightly stronger PRS-only AUC with far stronger validation-scale support. No other candidate shows a clearly better-supported combination of endpoint alignment + PRS-only performance + validation support: PGS004861/PGS004862 have very large validation but only full-model AUROC/R² (not clearly PRS-only), and PGS004946/PGS004947/PGS004948/PGS004950 have weaker PRS-only AUCs (0.64–0.66) or smaller validation in the EUR clinical subset. Therefore keep PGS004949.

TRIAGE: Plan: compare across three main endpoint clusters and keep both (a) strongest apparent predictive evidence and (b) cleaner/alternative siblings for head-to-head.

1) Direct heart failure / I50 heart failure endpoints (keep for endpoint fidelity):
- PGS001790 (Heart failure; PRS-CS-auto) has explicit PRS-only R2 plus a reported AUROC (though appears full-model packaged with covariates). Large validation N and multi-cohort context make it a key anchor despite metric packaging ambiguity.
- PGS000709 (Heart failure; snpnet multi-PRS) reports time-to-event C-index and HR with conventional covariates; strong sample sizes and direct endpoint.
- PGS005097 (Heart failure; PRS-CSx) reports AUROC with CI and Brier skill score; phenotype is prevalent HF and validation ancestry label is less clear, but it is a recent, direct-endpoint candidate worth close comparison.
- PGS004532 vs PGS004462 (both I50 heart failure; same paper family) are important to compare because they share endpoint and evaluation setting but differ by method (metaPRS integration vs disease PRS) and effect size magnitude; covariates/metric details are sparse so they can mislead a single-shot picker.
- PGS003969 (Heart failure; 39 GWS SNPs) has a clear OR with CI and direct endpoint; despite low variant count and missing covariate detail, it’s a plausible “simple but robust” comparator.

2) Congestive heart failure (PheCode 428.1) family with many near-ties (risk of being misled by tiny metric differences):
- Shortlist the apparent top performers by reported C-index and OR: PGS005083, PGS005077, PGS005080, PGS005076, PGS005074. These are near-tied siblings (same publication, similar covariates, similar variant counts) where downstream comparison should focus on endpoint definition, metric type consistency, and whether the reported performance is PRS-only vs packaged.
- Keep remaining siblings on watchlist (PGS005073/075/078/079/081/082/084/085) because they are method variants within the same study; small differences could flip depending on which metric/ancestry slice is prioritized.

3) Congestive heart failure (nonhypertensive) / pulmonary heart disease (cor pulmonale) portability set (adjacent endpoints; cleaner portability framing but not exact target):
- Keep PGS001842 and PGS002051 on shortlist as the closest-to-target within that portability paper (congestive HF) with partial-r reported across multiple ancestries; useful as a portability/robustness comparator even though metric is partial correlation rather than AUC.
- Keep PGS001840 and PGS002049 on watchlist as pulmonary-heart-disease variants (less endpoint-aligned) that could look better on partial-r but are not the same phenotype.

4) NPJ Genomic Medicine 2025 LDpred2 set (prevalent HF; multiple closely related records):
- Keep all on watchlist (PGS005299–PGS005306, plus PGS005301/PGS005305) because they are internally comparable (same paper family, similar covariates, AUROC/R2 reported) and could be tempting due to cleaner reporting, but their reported AUROCs are visibly lower than several other candidates and validation Ns vary; still worth having available for downstream head-to-head if endpoint (prevalent HF) is prioritized.

5) Context-specific incident HF scores (possible misleading specificity):
- PGS005319 and PGS004598 are incident HF in specific subpopulations/settings with HRs; keep on watchlist because they may not generalize to the broad target trait even if effect sizes look decent.

Overall: shortlist includes (a) direct HF/I50 candidates with the strongest/most interpretable predictive evidence, (b) the top CHF PheCode siblings plus a few method variants to avoid overfitting to one metric snapshot, and (c) the closest portability-paper CHF scores as robustness comparators. Watchlist retains near-tied siblings and context-specific or less-aligned endpoints that could otherwise mislead a single-shot selection. Uncertainty: Many candidates report full-model AUROC/C-index (with covariates) rather than PRS-only metrics, making cross-record comparability uncertain; several families (HGG Adv CHF PheCode set; NPJ Genom Med LDpred2 set; Commun Biol I50 set) contain near-duplicate siblings where tiny metric differences may not be meaningful. Endpoint heterogeneity (heart failure vs prevalent HF vs incident HF vs CHF PheCode vs nonhypertensive CHF vs pulmonary heart disease) is a major source of ambiguity; downstream comparison should explicitly stratify by endpoint definition rather than assuming all are interchangeable. LEGACY_PROPOSAL: Multiple direct-match candidates exist for the target trait (heart failure), including several exact heart-failure endpoints (e.g., PGS000709, PGS001790, PGS003969, PGS005097, PGS005299–PGS005306) and several congestive heart failure phecode endpoints (PGS005073–PGS005085). Among these, PGS005097 is best supported by a combination of (i) clear phenotype alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo = heart failure; phenotyping_reported = prevalent heart failure), (ii) a disease-focused multi-cohort development context (training_development_cohorts includes multiple HF-relevant biobanks/consortia such as HERMES, MVP, FinnGen, etc., consistent with a dedicated HF genetics study), and (iii) reported discrimination (full-model AUROC 0.72 with Brier skill score reported). However, the choice remains sub-optimal because most candidates lack PRS-only (covariate-isolated) metrics, making cross-model performance comparisons uncertain; additionally, some competing CHF models report higher full-model C-index (~0.753) but are from a methods-comparison paper with unclear PRS-only contribution and a different endpoint label (congestive HF phecode), so the evidence does not cleanly identify a single unequivocal winner. PICK: Revising the legacy prior (PGS005097) because the HGG Adv CHF (PheCode 428.1) family contains multiple direct-match candidates with visibly stronger discrimination/effect evidence under ordinary covariate packaging, and the differences are large enough to be meaningful even though metrics are full-model packaged.

PGS005077 (ldpred; CHF NOS PheCode 428.1) is the best-supported direct-match among the full candidate list on the visible evidence: it reports one of the top discrimination estimates in the entire set (full-model C-index 0.7536) alongside a strong effect size (OR 1.452, 95% CI 1.38–1.53) with conventional covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs) and a clear evaluation sample size (n=31,804; European slice shown). Within its near-duplicate sibling set (PGS005073–PGS005085), it is essentially tied for best C-index and among the strongest ORs.

Why not keep PGS005097: although it is a cleanly labeled heart-failure endpoint from a dedicated multi-cohort study and reports AUROC 0.72 (with CI) plus Brier skill score, its reported discrimination is lower than the top CHF PheCode models here, and its validation ancestry label is less crisp ("European, African unspecified") with a smaller validation N (n=40,989) than some other large-scale HF records; overall, the HGG Adv CHF models provide stronger visible predictive signal with similarly ordinary covariate packaging.

Why still sub-optimal: the top-performing CHF PheCode records are from a methods-comparison paper and report full-model C-index/OR rather than PRS-only AUC/R2, and the endpoint label (CHF PheCode) is not identical to the broader "heart failure" label used by other candidates (e.g., PGS001790/PGS000709/PGS005097). This makes the winner defensible but not unequivocal. CRITIC: Revision is warranted because the proposed_pick (PGS005077) is not as endpoint-aligned to the target trait label as several visible direct heart-failure records, and the claimed superiority is not a clean visible comparison.

Key visible contradiction in the proposed rationale: it treats the CHF PheCode 428.1 family as a straightforward “direct-match” replacement for heart failure and compares its full-model C-index (~0.7536) against PGS005097’s AUROC (0.72). These are different discrimination metrics (C-index vs AUROC) and come from different modeling contexts; the records do not provide PRS-only metrics for the CHF PheCode models, so the apparent advantage is not securely attributable to the PGS itself.

Endpoint fidelity: PGS005097 has trait_reported/trait_efo = Heart failure and phenotyping_reported = Prevalent heart failure, matching the target trait label directly. PGS005077 is labeled “Congestive heart failure (CHF), NOS (PheCode 428.1)”, which is close but not identical; given the lack of PRS-only metrics and the metric-type mismatch, this endpoint shift is not justified by stronger, directly comparable evidence.

Support strength among direct HF candidates: PGS005097 provides AUROC with CI plus Brier skill score and comes from a dedicated multi-cohort HF genetics context with conventional covariates. Other direct HF options either have weaker/older discrimination (e.g., PGS000709 C-index 0.635), lower AUROC (PGS005299–PGS005306 ~0.57–0.63), or less complete covariate/performance context (e.g., PGS003969 OR only; PGS004462/PGS004532 OR only; covariates unknown).

Legacy vs proposed: The legacy pick (PGS005097) remains more defensible on visible evidence because it is the strongest-supported, directly labeled heart-failure endpoint with explicit discrimination + calibration-type reporting, whereas the proposed CHF PheCode pick relies on non-comparable metrics and does not clearly isolate PRS contribution.

TRIAGE: Shortlist focuses on candidates with (a) direct hip OA / coxarthrosis endpoint alignment and (b) some interpretable predictive evidence (AUC/C-index/HR/OR) and/or strong model scale that could plausibly win head-to-head.

- PGS000967: Direct hip coxarthrosis TTE endpoint; reports both PRS-only and full-model AUC/R² plus incremental AUC with conventional covariates. Even if full-model metrics are not PRS-only, the presence of PRS-only AUC/R² makes it a key “clean-metric” comparator.
- PGS002728: Hip OA framed via total hip replacement; has an AUROC with CI (age/sex covariates). Endpoint is a proxy/advanced-disease definition but still tightly related and has interpretable discrimination evidence; could look competitive vs other AUC/C-index-reported models.
- PGS004882: Incident hip OA with very large validation N and time-to-event framing (C-index) plus HR. Metrics aren’t PRS-only, but the scale and endpoint framing could mislead a single-shot picker (big N, survival metric) and therefore deserves direct comparison against PGS000967/PGS002728.
- PGS002763: Hip OA with very large variant count (PRS-CS) and a relatively strong OR with CI; lacks AUC/C-index but could outperform in risk-gradient terms. Important near-tie candidate because it’s a different method family and reports a clear effect size.

Watchlist retains plausible alternatives and “sibling” models where limited/unclear reporting could otherwise cause over- or under-selection:
- PGS002750: Total hip replacement endpoint with OR and CI but small validation N and no AUC; could be misleadingly attractive due to endpoint specificity while being underpowered/less comparable.
- PGS004478 & PGS004548: Same publication family and same phenotype label (M16 coxarthrosis) with large variant counts; only single-point ORs and covariates listed as unknown. They could be strong but are hard to compare on the visible metrics; keep for downstream inspection rather than dropping. Uncertainty: Comparability is limited by heterogeneous metric types (AUROC vs C-index vs OR/HR) and inconsistent separation of PRS-only vs covariate-adjusted performance across records. Several candidates have strong endpoint alignment but sparse performance reporting (notably PGS004478/PGS004548), so they remain plausible despite being hard to rank at triage. LEGACY_PROPOSAL: All 7 candidates are direct matches at the disease-concept level (hip osteoarthritis / coxarthrosis / hip OA-related arthroplasty endpoints). The strongest endpoint-fidelity candidates for generic hip osteoarthritis are those with phenotyping_reported explicitly as hip osteoarthritis (PGS002763) or incident hip osteoarthritis (PGS004882), whereas total hip replacement/arthroplasty (PGS002728, PGS002750) is a treatment/proxy endpoint and time-to-event coxarthrosis (PGS000967) is a less standard endpoint and comes from a pan-trait UKB framework paper (a negative signal per domain knowledge).
